strengths: Presentation is generally clear and polished: the mechanism is explained with equations and an algorithm, limitations are stated explicitly, and the experiments span image classification, autoregressive generation, and language understanding.

The empirical results are promising under the reported protocols. KViT improves every matched ViT result while reducing reported FLOPs; KARM improves BPD over full attention on MNIST and CIFAR-10 while increasing throughput; and the hybrid Llama/Qwen models often outperform their LoRA baselines.

The component ablations are useful. Tables 13, 15, and 16 separately examine the RBF kernel, locality, top-k selection, and efficiency-quality tradeoffs. The Swin experiment also attempts to distinguish the kernel from locality alone.

The proposed combination of distance-based affinities, local neighborhoods, and adaptive top-k interactions is potentially useful, even though its components and the resulting RBF attention rule have substantial precedent.

The limitations and impact discussions are appropriate and do not reveal a material research-ethics concern. The paper correctly acknowledges that its theory is idealized and that LLM experiments only add an auxiliary pathway rather than replacing attention.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central bounded-confidence interpretation does not match the implemented operator. Positional/causal windows are not confidence sets in representation space, and top-k always selects k elements regardless of their absolute distance. Thus the assertion in Eq. 21 that the method induces a fixed distance cutoff R is not established. Consequently, the theoretical conclusions do not directly apply to Algorithm 1.

The mean-field analysis is technically unsupported. Equation 22 omits the row-normalization denominator present in the actual attention rule; the top-k support is state- and measure-dependent and discontinuous; and ||Qx-Ky|| generally yields an asymmetric kernel when Q and K differ, undermining the stated symmetric interaction energy and Wasserstein-gradient-flow derivation. Moreover, the analysis assumes that separated clusters already exist, then infers their persistence; it does not prove that the implemented method creates them. The claim that intra-cluster, tangential motion prevents clusters from later approaching is also not justified.

The claimed computational advantage of the RBF kernel is questionable. After row normalization, exp(-||q-k||²/(2σ²)) is equivalent to softmax attention with a scaled q·k term and a key-norm bias, so it does not avoid query-key inner products or exponential normalization. The claim that this kernel alone more than halves Swin FLOPs therefore requires a precise operation count and implementation benchmark. Algorithm 1 also appears to compute pairwise distances before masking; linear complexity requires a specialized windowed computation that is not specified. Top-k costs and memory are omitted.

The evaluation lacks key controls. Vision experiments do not compare against matched local-window or top-k dot-product attention, so improvements attributed to Krause dynamics may instead come from ordinary locality or sparsity. The LLM model adds a parallel trainable pathway and slightly more adapter parameters, but there is no capacity-matched auxiliary-attention control. The attention-sink evidence is largely tautological because a finite causal window mechanically prevents distant tokens from attending to the first token; it does not demonstrate reduced collapse in the remaining standard-attention pathway or causally connect sink reduction to task gains.

Reported results have no number of seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests despite some small improvements. Hyperparameter-selection protocols are unspecified, and multiple LLM window/top-k configurations are evaluated on the reported benchmark suite, raising selection concerns. The ImageNet ViT baselines are also substantially below strong established training recipes, limiting the significance of the absolute results.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper provides many optimizer settings but no code, seeds, exact model/configuration definitions, implementation details for efficient windowed distance computation, FLOP-counting methodology, software versions, or complete preprocessing/evaluation procedures. These omissions are especially consequential because the surprising FLOP claims cannot be independently audited from the manuscript.

Originality is overstated. Normalized RBF attention reduces algebraically to a close variant of softmax dot-product attention with a key-norm term, while local-window and top-k sparse attention are established ideas. The Krause framing could offer new understanding, but the current theoretical mismatch prevents it from substantiating that originality.

Presentation overstates evidence in several places: qualitative heatmaps are described as visually confirming global consensus and multi-cluster dynamics without quantitative representation-diversity or clustering metrics, and attention sinks are asserted to be a manifestation of representation collapse without a demonstrated theoretical or empirical equivalence. These unsupported central claims outweigh the otherwise broad empirical study.

strengths: The proposed Gaussian/RBF attention with local windows and top-k selection is intuitive, easy to integrate into Transformer blocks, and potentially useful as an efficiency-oriented inductive bias.

The empirical scope is broad: the paper studies image classification, autoregressive image generation, and auxiliary pathways in two LLM families. It also reports component ablations, likelihood results, measured throughput, FLOPs, and several training recipes.

The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished. The appendix openly acknowledges that the theory is idealized, that hyperparameters are task-dependent, and that the LLM experiments do not replace or pretrain the original attention mechanism.

The experiments report several promising results, including consistent improvements over the authors' vanilla ViT baselines and a likelihood/throughput trade-off superior to full attention in the autoregressive image experiments. No distinctive research-ethics concern is apparent beyond the usual impacts of improving general-purpose models.
weaknesses: The central theoretical identification with bounded-confidence dynamics is not sound for the implemented method. Local neighborhoods are defined by spatial or causal position, while top-k always retains k elements regardless of their representation distance. Neither operation supplies a confidence-radius cutoff. Consequently, the assertion in Eq. 21 that the resulting kernel has compact support in query-key distance does not follow from the algorithm, undermining the mean-field analysis.

The multi-cluster results largely assume the desired conclusion. Appendix C begins after tokens have already fragmented into permanently disconnected groups and then shows that disconnected groups remain independent. It does not establish that the proposed finite-depth network creates such groups. Moreover, the claim that supports remain invariant is asserted without controlling their evolution, the time-varying top-k graph, or distinct learned Q and K maps. Perron-Frobenius properties of an instantaneous stochastic matrix likewise do not by themselves prove convergence of the time-varying Transformer dynamics.

The claimed connection between global synchronization, representation collapse, and attention sinks is speculative rather than demonstrated. The paper provides no theorem connecting these phenomena and no quantitative representation-collapse or clustering metric. Attention heatmaps and first-token curves are insufficient, particularly because the LLM retains its original global-attention pathway; it is unclear whether Figure 7 measures the original pathway, the local auxiliary pathway, or an incommensurate combination.

Originality is limited and insufficiently situated experimentally. RBF attention is simply row normalization of exp(-||q-k||^2/(2 sigma^2)), equivalent to a softmax over negative squared distances and closely related to dot-product attention with norm-dependent terms. Combining this with standard local-window and top-k sparsity is reasonable, but the paper does not compare against strong local, sparse/top-k, Gaussian-distance, or modern efficient-attention baselines that would isolate what is specifically gained from the proposed formulation.

Several efficiency claims are technically questionable. Computing all pairwise Euclidean distances still requires O(d) work per pair and can be implemented using a QK product plus norm terms; it does not generally avoid expensive inner products as claimed. Top-k selection does not reduce the cost of first scoring all W candidates and itself incurs overhead. The reported FLOP reductions, especially for dense RBF attention and windowed Swin models, are therefore not adequately derived or validated with memory and training-time measurements.

The evaluation does not convincingly support broad superiority. Vision comparisons rely mainly on relatively weak vanilla ViT baselines, with no competitive modern architectures or matched local-attention control. Generation gains in BPD are small and lack uncertainty estimates. LLM improvements confound the proposed mechanism with an added parallel trainable pathway and increased parameters; there is no matched-capacity shortcut control, multiple-seed analysis, or end-to-end language-modeling evaluation. Some base-model scores, such as near-random PIQA results, are unexpectedly poor and call the evaluation pipeline into question.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The paper provides useful optimizer-level recipes but no code or checkpoints, random seeds, variance across runs, exact construction and seed of the 50K Flan-v2 subset, model/configuration details sufficient to reconstruct every baseline, or rigorous definitions for the attention visualizations and FLOP accounting. Reporting several LLM hyperparameter configurations without a specified validation-selection protocol also leaves room for test-set selection.

Presentation repeatedly overstates what the evidence establishes, using terms such as 'rigorously sustaining,' 'fundamentally alters,' and 'visually confirms' despite conditional theory and qualitative plots. There are also notation problems, including the ill-defined neighborhood expression xi_x(y) in Eq. 20 and an inconsistent distance definition between Eq. 5 and Algorithm 1. The limitations section is welcome but does not acknowledge the core mismatch between the implemented positional/top-k support and the assumed representation-distance cutoff.

strengths: The proposed combination of RBF query-key affinities, local windows, and adaptive top-k interactions is intuitive and easy to integrate into Transformer architectures. The bounded-confidence perspective is an interesting conceptual lens, even though the formal connection is not established convincingly.

The empirical study spans image classification, autoregressive image generation, and two 7B–8B language models. Reported gains are consistent across the evaluated configurations; for example, KViTs improve accuracy while reporting lower FLOPs, and KARMs improve BPD and throughput over full-attention ARMs.

The component ablations, window/top-k sensitivity studies, model configurations, training recipes, parameter counts, and hardware information are useful. The hybrid LLM experiments also report inference throughput and distinguish their setting from full attention replacement.

The manuscript is polished and well organized, with clear motivation, readable figures, and an honest limitations section covering the idealized theory, task-dependent hyperparameters, and restricted form of LLM integration. The impact statement identifies no distinctive ethical risk, which is reasonable for this architectural work.
weaknesses: The central bounded-confidence interpretation is not supported by the actual mechanism. Spatial or causal windows impose locality in token-index space, while top-k always retains k neighbors regardless of their representation distance. Neither implements the fixed distance-radius cutoff of the Krause model. Thus the method is more accurately an RBF-weighted local top-k attention rule than a direct bounded-confidence interaction process.

The appendix's theoretical conclusions do not follow from the stated model. It assumes already-separated, disconnected clusters and then proves persistence, rather than showing that the proposed dynamics create them. Moreover, disconnection under a state-dependent top-k graph need not remain invariant. The claim that locally determined tangential velocities prevent supports from approaching another cluster is also unsupported.

The mean-field gradient-flow derivation appears technically incorrect for the proposed attention. With general learned Q and K, the gradient of exp(-||Qx-Ky||^2/(2 sigma^2)) is not the stated projected-y velocity field; the kernel can be asymmetric, and the directed, measure-dependent top-k operator further obstructs the asserted pairwise-energy gradient-flow formulation. Consequently, the multi-cluster convergence result and its claimed applicability to the implemented Transformer are not established.

The attention-sink evidence is insufficient for the causal claims. It consists mainly of qualitative first-token curves, without aggregate sink metrics across examples, heads, and tokens, representation-collapse measurements, or a matched LoRA/local-attention control. A local pathway suppressing access to distant initial tokens does so largely by construction, and the paper does not isolate this effect from the claimed synchronization mechanism.

Efficiency comparisons are not adequately substantiated. Squared Euclidean query-key distance still requires a query-key inner product (plus norm and exponential operations), so the claim that the RBF kernel avoids expensive inner products is incorrect. Top-k also does not eliminate computation of scores for all W candidates. Reported FLOP reductions may omit distance, masking, or selection operations, and no matched local dot-product baseline or vision wall-clock/memory benchmark is provided.

The empirical baselines do not isolate the contribution or establish competitiveness. Vision comparisons are primarily against unusually weak globally attentive ViTs, image generation uses only full attention and one linear-attention baseline, and the LLM method adds a second pathway and extra trainable parameters without comparisons to parameter-matched local, RBF, top-k, or gated-attention alternatives. Several improvements are small, yet results use single point estimates with no seeds, variability, or significance tests.

Reproducibility is only partial: many training hyperparameters are reported, but there is no code or pseudocode detailed enough to resolve implementation-critical issues such as efficient local-distance computation, top-k differentiation, boundary handling, learned mixing, and exact FLOP accounting. Random seeds and repeated-run statistics are also absent.

Originality is moderate rather than high because RBF attention, local windows, and top-k sparsification are established ingredients. The main novelty is their Krause-dynamics framing, but that framing currently overstates the mathematical correspondence. Correcting the theoretical mechanism and adding matched controls would require substantial revision rather than a minor clarification.
